benchmark_evaluations.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (RFC 2119)

criteria.name: Mandatory Requirement Definition
criteria.description: Evaluates the precise definition and interpretation of mandatory requirement terms (MUST, REQUIRED, SHALL) as absolute requirements.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Check whether MUST, REQUIRED, and SHALL are correctly defined as absolute requirements.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: 1. MUST   This word, or the terms "REQUIRED" or "SHALL", mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification.

criteria.name: Prohibition Definition
criteria.description: Evaluates the definition of prohibition terms (MUST NOT, SHALL NOT) as absolute restrictions.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Inspect whether MUST NOT and SHALL NOT are defined as absolute prohibitions.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: 2. MUST NOT   This phrase, or the phrase "SHALL NOT", mean that the definition is an absolute prohibition of the specification.

criteria.name: Conditional Recommendation and Exception Handling
criteria.description: Evaluates the nuanced definitions of SHOULD and SHOULD NOT regarding valid reasons for deviation and implication awareness.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Check whether the conditions and implications for ignoring SHOULD or implementing SHOULD NOT behaviors are clearly explained.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: 3. SHOULD   This word, or the adjective "RECOMMENDED", mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course.

criteria.name: Optionality and Interoperability Management
criteria.description: Evaluates how MAY and OPTIONAL are defined, specifically concerning mandatory interoperability regardless of whether an option is included or omitted.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Verify that implementations including or omitting options are explicitly required to remain interoperable.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: An implementation which does not include a particular option MUST be prepared to interoperate with another implementation which does include the option, though perhaps with reduced functionality.

criteria.name: Guidance on Imperative Usage
criteria.description: Evaluates instructions regarding the careful, sparse use of requirement imperatives strictly for interoperation or harm limitation.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Inspect whether instructions prohibit using imperatives to impose methods not required for interoperability.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly.  In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm

criteria.name: Security Implications Elaboration
criteria.description: Evaluates the requirement for document authors to explicitly elaborate on security implications when requirements or recommendations are bypassed.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Check if authors are instructed to detail security effects when failing to implement MUST or SHOULD directives.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: Document authors should take the time to elaborate the security implications of not following recommendations or requirements as most implementors will not have had the benefit of the experience and discussion that produced the specification.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 31-72 provide precise, operational definitions for all 10 keywords. For example, L31-32: "1. MUST This word, or the terms 'REQUIRED' or 'SHALL', mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification." And L43-46 for SHOULD: "there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course."
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The submission exhaustively defines all required normative keywords (MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, OPTIONAL) and clearly distinguishes absolute requirements from recommendations and optional features, including interoperability requirements for options.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: 1. MUST This word, or the terms "REQUIRED" or "SHALL", mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 20-26 explicitly instruct: "Authors who follow these guidelines should incorporate this phrase near the beginning of their document: The key words 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', 'MAY', and 'OPTIONAL' in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119."
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The document provides explicit, exact copy-pasteable boilerplate text and gives clear instructions on its location near the beginning of the document.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt:
Authors who follow these guidelines should incorporate this phrase near the beginning of their document:

      The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL
      NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED",  "MAY", and
      "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in
      RFC 2119.

criteria_details.criterion_name: Guidance on Proper Imperative Usage and Restraint
criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 74-95 (Section 6 "Guidance in the use of these Imperatives") state: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm...". Deducted 0.5 because concrete examples of borderline misuse in actual RFC protocols could have further clarified edge cases.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: Section 6 explicitly cautions against the overuse of imperatives, stating they must be used with care and sparingly, and exclusively where required for interoperation or to limit behavior with potential for causing harm.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly.  In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm

criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 97-104 (Section 7 "Security Considerations") state: "These terms are frequently used to specify behavior with security implications. The effects on security of not implementing a MUST or a SHOULD, or doing something the procedure says MUST NOT or SHOULD NOT be done may be very subtle." Deducted 0.5 because the section is brief without concrete illustrative security failure modes.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: Section 7 details the security ramifications of non-compliance, explaining that ignoring MUST/SHOULD or violating MUST NOT/SHOULD NOT recommendations can create subtle security vulnerabilities and urges authors to elaborate on these implications.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: The effects on security of not implementing a MUST or SHOULD, or doing something the specification says MUST NOT or SHOULD NOT be done may be very subtle.

benchmark_evaluations.title: Towards a Verified Findel: Formal Semantics in Coq (arXiv:1909.05464)
benchmark_evaluations.domain: Formal Methods & Smart Contracts Academic Research Paper

criteria.name: Coq Formalization and Syntax Fidelity
criteria.description: Evaluates how accurately the syntax and primitives of the Findel domain-specific language are modeled and encoded in Coq.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Inspect Section 3.1 and Figure 1 for the Coq Inductive definition of Primitive and ensure it corresponds to Table 1.
criteria.evidence_excerpt:
Inductive Primitive :=
(* basic primitives *)
| Zero : Primitive
| One : Currency -> Primitive
(* composite primitives *)
| Scale : nat -> Primitive -> Primitive
| ScaleObs : Address -> Primitive -> Primitive
| Give : Primitive -> Primitive
| And : Primitive -> Primitive -> Primitive
| Or : Primitive -> Primitive -> Primitive
| If : Address -> Primitive -> Primitive -> Primitive
| Timebound : nat -> nat -> Primitive -> Primitive.

criteria.name: Marketplace Operational Semantics
criteria.description: Evaluates the formalization of the marketplace environment, including state components and transition rules such as [Issue], [Join], [Join OR], [Fail], and [Tick].
criteria.evidence_guidance: Examine Section 3.2 and the definitions of transition rules like [Issue], [Join], and [Fail].
criteria.evidence_excerpt: The marketplace (i.e., the environment where contracts are executed) is a tuple with several components ⟨C , D, B,t, G , i, L , E⟩ encoded as a record in Coq

criteria.name: Theorem Proving and Contract Property Verification
criteria.description: Evaluates the formulation and Coq proofs of specific properties and potential vulnerabilities for various Findel contracts (FRCE, EXT, and ZCB).
criteria.evidence_guidance: Review Section 4 and the stated theorems (Theorem 4.1 through Theorem 4.6) concerning fixed-rate currency exchange, external gateways, and zero-coupon bonds.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: Theorem 4.6. If ZCB is executed, then Bob can claim 11 dollars from Alice.

criteria.name: Meta-Properties and Soundness Argument
criteria.description: Evaluates the discussion of meta-properties of the Coq formalization, such as state consistency, ledger consistency, and time progression.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Inspect the conclusions section detailing the meta-properties of the formalization.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: The results shown in Section 4 use several meta-properties o f our Coq formalisation: (1) the step relation preserves state consistency; (2) event generatio n preserves states consistency; (3) the ledger is consistent; (4) parties cannot withdraw once they have agre ed to upon a contract; (5) the time passing is not affected by contract execution.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 11-15 state: "We present the first formal semantics of Findel - a DSL for specifying financial contracts... formalized in Coq". Section 3 details the primitive grammar (Give, Scale, One, Truncate, And, Or, If) and valuation semantics. Deducted 0.5 because some Coq proof lemmas are deferred to an external repository.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The paper presents a rigorous formalization of Findel's syntax and operational semantics in Coq, including the inductive definition of primitives, the recursive execution function 'exec', and formalized transition rules like [Issue], [Join], [Join OR], [Fail], and [Tick]. It demonstrates formal proofs of several theorems and lemmas regarding contract properties.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: In Coq, we provide a function called exec which executes primitives recursively. ... The marketplace (i.e., the environment where contracts are executed) is a tuple with several components ⟨C, D, B, t, G, i, L, E⟩ encoded as a record in Coq

criteria_details.human_feedback: Lines 21-35 and Section 2.1 demonstrate how European Call options, zero-coupon bonds, and portfolio swaps decompose cleanly into Findel primitives.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The submission models concrete financial derivatives such as fixed-rate currency exchanges (FRCE), external gateway rate currency exchanges (EXT), and zero-coupon bonds (ZCB) using Findel primitives, demonstrating the expressiveness of the DSL for real-world financial contracts.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt:
FRCE = And(Give(Scale(11, One(USD))), Scale(10, One(EUR)))
EXT = (And (Give (Scale n (One EUR))) (ScaleObs ADDR (Scale n (One USD))))
ZCB = (And (Give (Scale (One USD) 10)) (At (now + 1 yr) (Scale (One USD) 11)))

criteria_details.human_feedback: Section 3.2 defines the execution environment tuple (t, b, a, o) and proves ledger balance conservation. Deducted 0.5 because gas limits and transaction fee mechanics on Ethereum are left abstract.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The paper models the execution environment through a marketplace record containing balances, current timestamps, external gateways, ledgers, and events, and mentions meta-properties (e.g., step relation preserves state consistency, event generation preserves state consistency, ledger consistency). The current implementation of Findel does not enforce any constraints on the balances of the users that prevents them from building up debt.

benchmark_evaluations.title: Scalable XML Collaborative Editing with Undo (arXiv:1010.3615)
benchmark_evaluations.domain: Distributed Systems / Collaborative Editing Academic Paper

criteria.name: CRDT Commutativity and Eventual Consistency
criteria.description: Evaluation of how well the proposed data type ensures that all concurrent operations commute, thereby achieving eventual consistency across replicas without complex concurrency control.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Examine the definitions of basic operations (Add, Del, SetAttr) and how timestamps and effect counters ensure independent commute properties.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: A Commutative Replicated Data Type(CRDT) [12] is a data type where all concurrent operations commute. In other words, whatever the delivery order of operations, the resulting document is identical. As a result, a CRDT ensure eventual consistency as proven in [12].

criteria.name: Global Selective Undo Mechanism
criteria.description: Assessment of the undo feature's capability to globally and selectively undo any operation from any user while preserving correctness from the user's perspective.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Check the effect counter mechanism, how undo and redo modify effect counters, and how visibility of XML elements and attributes is determined based on these counters.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: Then we count the effect counter of an operation : one minus the number of undo plus the number of redo. If this effect counter is greater than 0, the operation has an effect.

criteria.name: XML Tree and Attribute Handling
criteria.description: Evaluation of how the model captures all XML aspects including elements' children, attributes, and text contents using special attributes and unique identifiers.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Review how special attributes (@tag, @position, @text, @add, @del) and Last-Writer-Wins rules for attributes are structured.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: We consider an XML tree as an edge e with three elements : e.identifier the unique identifier of the edge (a timestamp), e.children the children of the edge (a set of edge), and e.attributes the attributes of the edge (a map string to value).

criteria.name: Garbage Collection and Scalability
criteria.description: Assessment of the garbage collection mechanism designed to safely purge old operation logs, tombstones, and redundant history without harming the global selective undo capability.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Inspect the vector-based clock minimum tracking and the specific purging rules defined for attribute values, delete timestamps, and add values.
criteria.evidence_excerpt: Thus, the time and space complexity of the approach is greatly reduced to be proportional to the size of the view. Moreover, differently to the RFC 677, replicas send mi − k with k a global constant instead of mi. Thus, even if the replicas are tightly synchronized — having mi very close to their own clock —, the replicas can always undo the last operations.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Sections 2 and 3 define node addressing and operation commutativity. Deducted 1.0 because concurrent move-cycle handling requires complex reordering heuristics that are only partially proved.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The submission provides a complete tree operation algebra (Add, Del, SetAttr) with identifiers and timestamps designed to maintain tree acyclicity and path validity. It incorporates mechanisms for ordering children using dense positions and handles attributes, special attributes (@tag, @position, @text), and delete/add tracking via effect counters.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt:
The basic operations that affect an XML tree are : 
– Add (idp,id) : Adds a edge with identiﬁer id under the edge idp. This edge is empty, it has no tag-name, child or attribute. 
– Del(id) : Deletes the edge identiﬁed by id. 
– SetAttr (id,attr,val,ts) : Sets the value val with the timestamp ts to the attribute attr of the edge identiﬁed by id.

criteria_details.criterion_name: Undo/Redo Semantic Correctness in Distributed Replicas
criteria_details.human_feedback: Defines selective and chronological undo mechanisms; acknowledges limitations when dependent operations have been executed by remote peers.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The paper defines a comprehensive selective undo mechanism using effect counters to track operations (one minus the number of undo plus the number of redo) and resolves concurrent undo/redo correctness scenarios. However, the formal mathematical proofs for convergence under arbitrary concurrent undos are explicitly deferred to a separate research report citation rather than fully proven within the text.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: To obtain a satisfying undo, we keep the information about every operations applied to each edge. Then we count the effect counter of an operation : one minus the number of undo plus the number of redo. If this effect counter is greater than 0, the operation has an effect.
criteria_details.ai_uncertainty: Formal proofs are referenced externally in a research report rather than fully detailed in the paper.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Section 5 provides experimental benchmarks across document sizes, but formal asymptotic bounds for deep nested trees are somewhat sparse.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The submission discusses log garbage collection, state vectors/clocks, and mentions that time and space complexity are reduced proportionally to the size of the view after garbage collection, but it lacks rigorous asymptotic time/space bounds (Big-O notation) for the transformation matrix or broad operational broadcasts.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: Thus, the time and space complexity of the approach is greatly reduced to be proportional to the size of the view.
criteria_details.ai_uncertainty: Explicit asymptotic Big-O bounds are missing.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Evaluates with simulated user traces over large XML documents, reporting millisecond response times and memory scaling.
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The paper provides no empirical benchmarks, latency simulations, real-world editing traces, or memory footprint evaluations, noting in the conclusion that experiments are left for future work.
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: Firstly, we need to make experiments to establish the actual scalability and efﬁciency of the approach in presence of huge data.
criteria_details.ai_uncertainty: No experimental results or performance evaluations are included in this short paper.

criteria_details.human_feedback: Strong bibliography citing canonical collaborative editing papers (Sun, Ellis, Ressel, Ignat).
criteria_details.ai_reasoning: The paper demonstrates strong citation rigor and positions its work thoroughly against relevant literature, including classical Operational Transformation (OT) approaches, CRDT foundations (Preguica et al., Shapiro, Letia), and prior XML replication and collaborative editing mechanisms (Ellis & Gibbs, Sun, Ressel, Ignat, Martin et al.).
criteria_details.ai_evidence_excerpt: The Operational Transformation (OT) [13] approach is an operation-based replication mechanism... Commutative Replicated Data Types [12,16] (CRDT) is a promising new class of algorithms...

criteria.name: Algorithm Optimization and Efficiency
criteria.description: Evaluates algorithmic choices made to minimize redundant comparisons, such as the specialized siftdown/siftup implementations described by Knuth.
criteria.evidence_guidance: Examine _siftup and its design rationale regarding comparisons during heap pops and heapifications.
criteria.evidence_excerpt:
def _siftup(heap, pos):
    endpos = len(heap)
    startpos = pos
    newitem = heap[pos]
    # Bubble up the smaller child until hitting a leaf.
    childpos = 2*pos + 1    # leftmost child position
    while childpos < endpos:
        # Set childpos to index of smaller child.
        rightpos = childpos + 1
        if rightpos < endpos and not heap[childpos] < heap[rightpos]:
            childpos = rightpos
        # Move the smaller child up.
        heap[pos] = heap[childpos]
        pos = childpos
        childpos = 2*pos + 1

It correctly handles sift-down and sift-up operations, heapify, and heap push/pop routines, maintaining the invariant a[k] <= a[2*k+1] and a[k] <= a[2*k+2].

def _siftdown(heap, startpos, pos):
    newitem = heap[pos]
    while pos > startpos:
        parentpos = (pos - 1) >> 1
        parent = heap[parentpos]
        if newitem < parent:
            heap[pos] = parent
            pos = parentpos
            continue
        break
    heap[pos] = newitem
